    The 10 Best Ways to Use Your Grandma’s Favorite $5 Cleaner

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • According to recent reports, as a gas, ammonia, hydrogen and nitrogen chemical compound is pungent and dangerous.
    • Before you buy ammonia, know that there are various types of household ammonia to choose from.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    According to recent reports, as a gas, ammonia, hydrogen and nitrogen chemical compound is pungent and dangerous. But in its diluted household form, the nitrogen-based super cleaner is a workhorse in the war on common household dirt and grime. Ammonia is readily available, inexpensive, and potent, so a little goes a long way.

    Before you buy ammonia, know that there are various types of household ammonia to choose from. You may see “cloudy” or “sudsy” versions—that’s ammonia with soap added, which is generally used for such domestic cleaning chores as treating stained clothing or scrubbing stovetops. We recommend opting for “clear” ammonia, which is suited to a wider variety of tasks (and you can always add a tablespoon or two of dish soap to make clear ammonia sudsy). You’ll also find ammonia that’s scented with lemon or pine to temper its stinging odor.

    In a recent development, the harsh smell serves as a warning, though: Working with ammonia absolutely requires caution. Pure chemical ammonia can cause severe burns and respiratory challenges if it comes into contact with skin or is ingested. Even diluted in water, as is recommended for most cleaning purposes, ammonia can still be harmful.

    Mixing ammonia and chlorine bleach creates a toxic gas called chloramine. Take great care not to combine them—doing so could have dire consequences.

    The most important safety rule to remember is: Never mix ammonia with chlorine bleach. The result is a highly toxic chlorine gas that can produce headaches, seizures, and other symptoms. It’s crucial to keep this in mind if you’re using ammonia with laundry or to clean surfaces. You want to make absolutely sure not to mix it with a detergent or household cleaner that contains bleach.

    When using ammonia, be sure to wear chemical-resistant gloves and ventilate the area well. Be sure, too, to store it where pets and children can’t access it. Bearing these safety guidelines in mind, put ammonia to work around the home, as generations have done before us.

    To achieve streak-free mirrors, windows, and crystal, mix 1 tablespoon clear ammonia with 2 cups water in a spray bottle. Spritz the solution onto glass items and wipe immediately with a soft, lint-free cloth for windows and crystal; paper towels work fine for mirrors.

    To remove stains on a concrete driveway, garage floor, or patio, mix 1 cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and apply it to the stain with a mop or large sponge. Let sit for about 20 minutes, and then scrub the stain with a bristled brush. Rinse the surface with clean water. If the stain isn’t completely gone after the area dries, repeat the process until you’re satisfied with the results.

    It has been revealed that if gold, silver, diamond, or platinum jewelry has lost its shine, mix 6 parts warm water to 1 part ammonia in a bowl (one that you don’t eat or cook with and add your jewelry. (Never use ammonia to clean pearls or other gems.) After 15 minutes, remove the jewelry with your gloved hand, and then gently scrape away any stubborn grime with a soft-bristled toothbrush (one that’s no longer in use or designated for cleaning). Allow it to soak for another 15 minutes, remove from the solution, and immediately rinse with warm water. Dispose of used ammonia solution down the drain while running the hot water. Polish the jewelry with a soft, lint-free cloth and let it dry.

    Stubborn stains on cotton, polyester, or nylon fabrics are no match for a solution of ⅔ cup clear ammonia, ⅔ cup dish soap, 6 tablespoons of baking soda, and 2 cups warm water. Mix in a bowl or bucket and apply generously to stains with a sponge or spray bottle. Let the treatment sit for about 30 minutes, then launder as usual. For tougher stains like blood or grass, treat the stain again with a solution of 1 part ammonia and 1 part warm water.

    Sources indicate that note: Do not use ammonia on wool or silk, which can eat through the delicate fabrics. And remember never to mix ammonia with any laundry products that contain bleach.

    According to recent reports, tackle caked-on grease on stove burners with this trick. Place each burner in a separate sealable plastic bag filled with ¼ cup ammonia. Seal each bag to keep fumes at bay, and place in a sink or washtub for 8 to 12 hours. Open the bags in a ventilated area, and remove all grease and dirt easily with a quick scrub of dish soap and water. Once the gunk is gone, thoroughly rinse the burners with water to get rid of ammonia residue. Let dry completely before using.

    Sources indicate that mix one part clear ammonia and one part hot water in a sprayer or other bottle. Apply generously to the stain by spritzing or with a sponge. After about 10 minutes of dwell time, place a clean old towel over the stain and press with an iron, blasting with steam, for about 20 seconds. Check your progress: The stain should start transferring to the towel. Repeat, with steam ironing and more ammonia solution if needed, until the stain is gone.

    Ammonia is tough on every odor from fresh paint to burnt lasagna. Place a small container filled with about 1/2 cup of clear ammonia near an offending smell, being sure to keep the area ventilated, to absorb the nastiness within hours.

    Heat the oven to 150 degrees, and set a large pot of water on the stove to boil. Turn off the oven and open the windows to ventilate the kitchen. Place a sturdy container, such as a glass measuring cup or metal bowl, filled with ½ cup ammonia on the oven’s top shelf. Place the pot of boiled water on the bottom shelf. Close the oven and let sit for 8 to 12 hours, then remove the containers of ammonia and water. Open the oven door and air air out for at least an hour before cleaning. Because the grime has basked in ammonia fumes, it should be loosened and easy to remove with a sponge, warm water, and dish soap.

    According to recent reports, this method is only recommended for electric ovens, because mixing ammonia with gas can be dangerous. If you choose to use this method on your gas oven, make sure that the pilot light and gas lines are turned off.

    To clean and disinfect kitchen and bath tiles, mix ¼ cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and use a sponge or mop to liberally apply the solution to the tile. Use a soft-bristled brush to scrub any particularly stubborn areas. Finish up by rinsing the surface with clean water and your sponge or mop.

    Recent findings suggest that ammonia’s strong scent can deter unwanted critters. Fill a saucer with clear, unscented ammonia, or saturate a rag or cotton balls with it. Then place in areas that attract pests, such as near garbage cans where raccoons prowl or beside cracks in the basement where mice enter. The smell will remind the varmints of predators, so they’re likely to catch a whiff and turn away, unharmed. That said, make sure to keep the ammonia deterrent out of reach of kids and pets.

    Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them.

    From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

    According to recent reports, tesla aims to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

    According to recent reports, tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The firm’s CEO Elon Musk claims Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

    Learn why the company is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

    Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images.

    It has been revealed that in a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”.

    Tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality problems, as well as several safety recalls.

    Sources indicate that current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

    For anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

    Tesla hasn’t mentioned which customers will receive their trucks or how it plans to handle the remaining orders.

    The Cybercab is Tesla’s two-seat electric car designed to drive itself. It doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals because it won’t need a human driver. Tesla has already started offering Cybercab rides in parts of Austin. The organization looks to expand the service, although the vehicles aren’t widely available yet.

    Musk denies that Tesla is ending production because the Cybertruck isn’t profitable. He says the organization can put its Texas factory to better use by making Cybercabs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    According to recent reports, should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

    In a recent development, before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the Fresh World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

    How many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

    If you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

    Definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” notes Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”.

    It has been revealed that it’s important to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”.

    It has been revealed that one option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she claims, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

    Industry observers note that if you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”.

    It has been revealed that for a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” notes Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”.

    This is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” indicates Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

    Sources indicate that the danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

    Before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

    Composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

    Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they promptly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”.

    Industry observers note that it’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

    Painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

    It has been revealed that if you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

    Full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

    Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

    A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

    Industry observers note that we considered numerous criteria when narrowing the field of wood stoves to these top selections. Build quality is crucial, so we only chose models with higher-gauge steel construction and forged-iron doors, except for our upgrade pick, which uses soapstone.

    Understanding the two types of wood stoves, the materials used to make them, and their heating capacity are all vital when shopping for one of these appliances. Ahead, learn more about these and other key attributes of the best wood stoves.

    Industry observers note that wood stoves are available in two types: catalytic and noncatalytic. Catalytic wood stoves differ from noncatalytic in that they produce fewer exhaust fumes and burn more efficiently. In addition to burning wood, catalytic wood stoves also have a combustor that burns smoke and byproducts. This design allows the stove to burn cleaner with a slower burn rate, conserving fuel. Efficiency ratings for a catalytic wood stove range between 63 and 84 percent, making them ideal options for use as a primary source of heat.

    Recent findings suggest that noncatalytic stoves are cheaper but not as efficient. They are better suited for use as a supplemental heater.

    Recent findings suggest that most wood stoves are made from one of three materials: cast iron, plate steel, or soapstone. Cast iron, the most commonly used material, heats up swiftly and retains warmth longer than other materials. However, it does crack more easily and is more expensive than other materials.

    Plate steel, also a common material used in wood stoves, is durable and retains heat well, though not as well as cast iron. Soapstone is a high-end material for wood stoves. It retains heat better than cast iron, burns cleaner than other materials, and can burn for 24 hours or longer on a single load. Most wood stoves consist of either soapstone or plate steel with a cast-iron door.

    It has been revealed that A wood stove’s heating capacity determines how large of a space the wood stove can keep warm when it’s running with a full load of wood. The heating area for most stoves ranges from around 1,200 square feet for a small stove to as much as 2,200 square feet (or more) for a large model.

    According to recent reports, keep in mind that, unlike a home’s central heating, which distributes heat through ductwork, a wood stove emanates heat from the fire, so the heat isn’t evenly distributed. The farther someone is from the wood stove, the cooler the temperature will be.

    The heat output of a wood stove is measured in BTUs (British thermal units). Wood stoves range in BTU output from around 50,000 to 80,000 BTUs. The more BTUs, the greater the size of the space the wood stove can heat. A large 70,000-BTU wood stove can warm up to 2,200 square feet. While BTU level is a great indication of how powerful the stove is, not all manufacturers provide BTU information for their stoves.

    A wood stove’s burn time is the amount of time one load of wood lasts before the stove requires reloading. Each stove’s burn time is determined by how much wood it can hold as well as the heat output of the stove, which can be regulated using the stove’s damper. The firewood type being used also affects burn time. Hardwoods burn more efficiently than softwood, which is less dense and therefore burns more swiftly and at lower temperatures.

    Wood-burning stoves produce toxic emissions; they create carbon monoxide, which can be deadly if not properly vented outside. Wood stoves are regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency, which performs safety tests on wood stoves to make sure they’re safe for consumer use. The emission limit for wood stoves is 2 grams to 2.5 grams per hour, depending on the type of wood. Catalytic stoves produce well under the EPA’s maximum, with emissions of around 0.5 grams per hour. Never buy a wood stove that is not certified by the EPA.

    It has been revealed that perhaps the most key thing to consider when shopping for a wood stove is where it will go in the living space. Most freestanding wood stoves take up a significant chunk of real estate since they measure about 3 feet wide and 2 feet deep and require a buffer around them for safety. Portable models are much smaller—about 20 inches high and 10 inches deep and less than 40 pounds—allowing them to fit in the trunk of a car for a camping trip.

    Keep in mind that the size of the stove also affects the size of wood they can burn. A standard freestanding or insert wood stove can hold logs up to 18 inches long, whereas portable models can typically handle logs that measure about 8 inches long.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to providing a source of heat, wood stoves also create an ambience that’s similar to a wood-burning fireplace. Most wood stoves have glass windows that allow people sitting around the stove to watch the burning logs.

    In a recent development, some wood stoves also serve as a cooking stove, with flat tops that will support a frying pan or pot. Stoves with cooking functions are typically designed for outdoor use and camping trips.

    In a recent development, the best place for a wood stove is as close to the center of the area requiring heat as possible. This allows the stove to radiate warmth in all directions, better heating the space.

    Sources indicate that hardwoods—which include oak, maple, ash, and birch—are the best-burning woods. They will burn longer and hotter than softwoods like pine and also contain the least amount of pitch and sap inside of them.

    Use a brush to sweep up any debris or ash that was not collected by the fireplace’s ash pan. Next, use a wire brush to clean off any buildup inside the flue pipe. Wipe off the exterior of the wood stove with a dry cloth. Be sure to avoid using liquids, which can leave streaks.

    The average wood stove should last between 10 and 20 years, depending on usage and care.

    Recent findings suggest that it is safe to leave a wood fireplace on overnight, as long as you follow a few precautions. Allow the wood to burn for a few hours before going to bed. Before turning in for the night, add ash to the burning logs to dampen the flames and slow the burning process. Next, close the stove air vents to reduce the size of the fire, ensuring it will be safe even when burning through the night.

    Yes. If the indoor wood-burning stove is not properly vented to the outside of the home, it can cause exhaust fumes to collect inside the home, resulting in carbon monoxide poisoning. If a wood-burning stove is installed properly, vented to the outside of the home, and EPA certified, it is safe to use.

    Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.
    • It has been revealed that what makes a yard an eyesore?
    • In a recent development, the good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

    It has been revealed that what makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

    In a recent development, the good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

    Unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can quickly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland says. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”.

    In a recent development, vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can quickly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception issue if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes indicates.

    It has been revealed that broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty says. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”.

    According to recent reports, fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be newly introduced to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker says. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”.

    Adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker notes. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”.

    Sources indicate that while low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes indicates. But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

    Industry observers note that A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes states. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

    “There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty claims. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

    Recent findings suggest that broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

    While they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland indicates. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

    “A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland says. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our newly introduced neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

    Kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty indicates. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

Weather-resistant lights can handle direct exposure to water and feature watertight seals to protect their interior components from accumulating moisture and causing safety challenges.

    When it comes to the appearance of outdoor string lights, brightness and color temperature are two of the most important factors to consider.

    It has been revealed that lumens measure the amount of light output from a bulb—the more lumens, the brighter the bulb. When deciding on bulb brightness, take into account the desired lighting effect. String light bulbs can range from 5 to more than 100 lumens per bulb. Customers often choose string lights for their glowy appearance rather than their brightness, so lower lumens often do just fine to set the mood. Lumens are different from wattage, as wattage measures how much power a bulb consumes and not necessarily how bright a light appears.

    Lighting color temperature is measured using the Kelvin temperature scale. This scale measures how warm or cool the light appears. Lower numbers on the Kelvin scale look warmer, and higher numbers look cooler.

    Sources indicate that most home lighting falls between 2000K and 6000K. Bulbs around 2700K have a cozy, warm white color with a yellow hue, while bulbs over 5000K offer stark, crisp lighting with a blue hue. Warm lighting makes a space look more cozy and inviting, while cool lighting can often appear harsh, especially at night. For this reason, warmer bulbs are generally preferred for ambient outdoor lighting.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1438 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    No Pseudonymity in Ex-Associate's Sexual Assault Claim Against Major Law Firm

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Blank Rome LLP, the opinion was issued under seal in May, but just unsealed last week (at my behest):.
    • It has been revealed that plaintiff is an attorney who filed a detailed, 197-paragraph Complaint under the pseudonym "Jane Doe" against Defendant Blank Rome LLP …, her former employer, alleging claims for sex discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation pursuant to Title VII ….
    • Sources indicate that doe's Complaint similarly details Associate A's professional background, including his law school and year of graduation, and the names of his prior law firms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From Judge W. Scott Hardy in Doe v. Blank Rome LLP, the opinion was issued under seal in May, but just unsealed last week (at my behest):.

    It has been revealed that plaintiff is an attorney who filed a detailed, 197-paragraph Complaint under the pseudonym "Jane Doe" against Defendant Blank Rome LLP …, her former employer, alleging claims for sex discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation pursuant to Title VII …. Her claims arise from the Firm's purported failure to respond appropriately after Doe allegedly was sexually assaulted by another associate attorney, identified in the Complaint as "Associate A," while they and others were socializing at the home of a Firm partner on a Saturday evening after leaving a graduation party hosted by another partner of the Firm. The Complaint details Doe's professional background, including where she attended law school, when she began her employment at the Firm, and the type of law she practiced while at the Firm.

    Sources indicate that doe's Complaint similarly details Associate A's professional background, including his law school and year of graduation, and the names of his prior law firms. The Complaint does not identify Doe by her own name, nor does it identify by name "Associate A" or any other attorney at the Firm. The only person identified by name in the Complaint is the Firm's Chief Human Resource Officer, who is named 24 times….

    The court noted the strong presumption in favor of parties litigating in their own names, and concludes this presumption wasn't rebutted here:.

    A mere showing of embarrassment or economic harm is not enough [to justify pseudonymity]. Rather, there must be a showing of both: (1) fear of severe harm, and (2) that the fear of severe harm is reasonable. When a litigant sufficiently alleges that he or she has a reasonable fear of severe harm from litigating without a pseudonym, the Third Circuit instructs that "district courts should balance the plaintiff's interest and fear against the public's strong interest in an open litigation process." {"[T]he Court is sympathetic to Plaintiff's concerns, and understands that, unfortunately, victims of sexual harassment and assault often face ridicule and further harassment when they file lawsuits or otherwise publicly disclose their allegations, especially in the internet age. However, these concerns, while certainly reasonable, are not sufficient to outweigh the public's right to access court proceedings."} ….

    It also expressed its concern about one-sided pseudonymity (a concern that some courts weigh heavily and others don't, as this article lays out in detail):.

    Industry observers note that doe is not the only party exposed to public humiliation and reputational harm. The Firm itself and its chief human resource officer have been identified publicly in the Complaint (and other current or former Firm attorneys have been described with sufficient identifying indicia in the Complaint to be identified by implication). Permitting Doe to proceed pseudonymously while the Firm defends itself publicly, particularly where there seems to be material factual disputes between the parties, presents an unfair asymmetry that also weighs against anonymity ….

    In a recent development, doe … plead[ed] highly detailed factual averments in her 197-paragraph Complaint that inform the reader of her law school, her prior law firm affiliation, the month and year she commenced work at the Firm, the general nature of her practice, and the date of her departure from the Firm. Similar factual averments were plead regarding Associate A, including by naming three firms at which Associate A had previously been employed. The Firm's identity has also been revealed both in the caption of the Complaint and in its detailed factual averments. Many of these averments supply indicia of identity of both Doe and Associate A even though they would not have been necessary pursuant to applicable pleading standards set forth in Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)…. [This] weighs against anonymity.

    In a recent development, the court also mentioned Doe's argument "that there are social stigmas that attach to victims of sexual assault and harassment, and that using her real name would subject her to 'ridicule, scrutiny, and alienation' by her own colleagues and would jeopardize her reputation within the local legal community," but responded that (1) "Doe is an adult, not a minor" and that (2) she "does not contend that she would forgo her claims if her motion to proceed pseudonymously were to be denied and there is no indication from the record that Doe would be deterred from proceeding if she identified herself." For whatever it's worth, plaintiff dismissed the case a few months after the decision denying pseudonymity, presumably pursuant to a settlement. Because of the dismissal, neither Doe nor Associate A were publicly identified in the docket.

    Finally, the court discussed in some detail the question "whether either party stakes out their respective positions here for illegitimate ulterior motives," a factor that some courts' multi-factor tests for pseudonymity mention but that rarely gets much elaboration:.

    Doe contends that the Firm would have no reason for opposing her motion other than her bald accusation that such opposition is being undertaken to "perpetuate ongoing harm" and to "further humiliate her, undermine her professional reputation and potentially deter her form continuing with this litigation." Doe proffers no particularized basis for this accusation beyond her objection that the Firm's General Counsel circulated an internal communication within the Firm itself about Doe at or near the time her Complaint was filed, to contend that the Firm opposes her pending motion for illegitimate and "nefarious" motives, further suggesting the Firm is opposing it as a "litigation tacti[c].".

    According to recent reports, for its part, the Firm similarly accuses Doe of illegitimate tactical motives for seeking to proceed pseudonymously despite filing a factually detailed Complaint with enough content for a reader to know or surmise the identities of its personnel so that she may "cast[] aspersions upon the character of others about whom she publicly alleges information that makes them readily identifiable." The Court notes, too, that Doe filed her detailed Complaint without seeking leave to file it under seal or in redacted form and did file it on the public docket approximately a week before seeking to proceed pseudonymously. {In saying so, the Court is not suggesting that proceeding in this manner is inappropriate or that that seeking to file such a pleading under seal or in redacted form is the better course. Though, there may be circumstances when doing so is advisable.}.

    On the present record, the Court discerns no illegitimate or nefarious motives by either party. In reaching this conclusion, the Court notes that there are known and anticipated vicissitudes and adversities to litigants involved in presumptively public judicial proceedings.

    According to recent reports, here, the Defendant is a large, multi-office law firm and Doe is one of its former lawyers. Both parties are experienced with the judiciary and presumably familiar with the reasonably foreseeable extrajudicial consequences litigation has on parties and witnesses.

    Industry observers note that moreover, lawyers representing their clients in court, such as counsel of record here, are expected to prepare and file pleadings and briefs on court dockets for legitimate purposes that subject them to potential sanctions if such filings are presented for an improper purpose. Of course, pleadings and briefs having a proper purpose may also have attendant collateral adverse extrajudicial consequences, but such consequences do not necessarily transform a proper filing into an improper one. Sometimes those boundaries are clear, sometimes blurred. {Here, on the present record, the Court detects some potential tactical and strategic efforts by both parties within the context of otherwise legitimate and proper lawyering but cautions both parties and their counsel to stay within those boundaries going forward.}.

    Sources indicate that as noted above, Doe has a legitimate interest in seeking to proceed pseudonymously to avoid potential embarrassment, humiliation, emotional distress, and professional reputational harm. Those are reasonable and understandable concerns. Likewise, the Firm's opposition to Doe's request is grounded on the desire for symmetry in the transparency of the Court's administration of justice so that Doe may not be permitted to "hurl accusations … from behind 'a cloak of anonymity.'" The Court agrees that such rationale, rooted in fairness and tethered to the presumption of transparency in court proceedings, is also reasonable and legitimate. Accordingly, the parties' respective motives neither favor nor disfavor Doe's continued anonymity.

    And the court concluded by noting "the presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings," and by saying that, "[w]hile the parties here are not public officials or public bodies, the strong presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings is not outweighed by the other … factors considered above.".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Sources indicate that your riding lawnmower can do double duty this winter by adding a snow plow. Here’s what you need to know before adding a plow to your riding mower.

    Snow is considered a “four-letter” word in our home. Living in the northeast, right in the middle of the so called “I-95” corridor, we usually average 20 inches of snow a year. Even with my trusted 26-inch two-stage snow blower and my newest gadget, an 18 volt snow shovel, clearing the driveway and sidewalk can rapidly turn into a significant time consuming and dangerous job. If you already own a riding mower (different from a lawn or garden tractor), you may wonder if you can add a snow plow to turn it into a useful piece of year-round equipment.

    The short answer is “yes, maybe,” said David Bodzioch, certified Small Engine and Automotive Technology Instructor. Snow (plow) blades are available for certain riding mowers. However, Bodzioch cautioned, “attaching a blade doesn’t necessarily make your mower ready to clean a snow-covered driveway.”.

    It has been revealed that accessory compatibility, traction, mower size as well as the amount and type of snow you typically need to move will determine if you can, or should, add a plow blade to your riding lawnmower. Before investing in a plow, you need to understand what your mower can realistically handle. As well as determining what accessories you might need. Here’s what our experts have to say about turning a riding mower into a snow plow.

    “Yes, many riding lawnmowers can be equipped with a front-mounted snow blade,” noted certified Small Engine instructor Jeffrey Cesari. “Even if aftermarket compatible attachments are available, you should use the manufacturer’s approved attachments,” added Cesari. “Adding a plow blade on small tractors requires a set of rear wheel chains and a counterweight for balance,” added Cesari.

    Industry observers note that for example, John Deere sells a front blade package (as well as snow throwers) designed for specific riding lawnmowers. A John Deer 19 horsepower or better twin-cylinder engine units position the driver closer to the engine for better balance.

    What Do You Need to Turn a Riding Lawnmower Into a Snow Plow?

    Sources indicate that “At minimum, you’ll need a snow blade and direct-fit mounting hardware designed to fit your particular make and model mower,” said Bodzioch. Tire chains and weights should also be considered when operating snow-clearing equipment. According to Troy-Bilt, makers of outdoor power equipment, “Depending on the riding lawnmower mower and snow conditions, the mower will benefit from the added traction that chains and weights provide” when removing snow.

    “It depends on whether your mower simply requires a blade, or the added cost of mounting hardware, weights and tire chains,” said Cesari. An add on blade can cost as little as $120 for 22 to 32 inch width universal riding mower plow kit, to over $1400 for a complete John Deere 46 inch front blade snow plow package that includes an adjustable three-position blade height and angle setting you can change from the driver’s seat. Look for heavy-gauge steel blades that are height-adjustable and have the ability to reposition the shave plate for longer life.

    Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage is getting year-round use from expensive equipment you already own. Plus, eliminating the need for another piece of snow-removal equipment that sits unused for nine or ten months out of the year.

    Recent findings suggest that “You’ll probably need to buy and install several accessories and that can be expensive,” remarked Bodzioch. You should also check how difficult it is swapping out the snow blade and grass cutting mower deck. He added that “you also want check if your mower and blade combination are right for your type [concrete, blacktop, etc.] driveway.”.

    Sources indicate that yes, it can be, and should be, as long as your mower is approved for the attachment, is well-maintained and in good working condition. Following the manufacturer’s operating, maintenance guides and safety instructions is mandatory for safe and efficient operation; the same as when using any other piece of outdoor power equipment.

    In a recent development, bodzioch noted, “Proper traction is especially important when driving on ice and snow, or on snow-covered grass or soil.” But Cesari also notes that “you need to be aware of frame structure and that adding a snow plow can cause frame damage, transmission wear and belt fatigue on small home riding mowers.” Cesari said plowing up to five inches should be safe. Always be cautious and use common sense if your mower is struggling while removing any amount of snow.

    Sources indicate that it depends. It may only make sense if you already own a compatible mower. However, having room and space to safely store the blade should be a real consideration. Cesari added, “Converting your mower to a plow may require buying expensive attachments or accessories. Consider a standalone snow blower or a lawn/garden tractor if it’s difficult swap out the mower deck and plow.” If you regularly deal with challenging snow conditions, a dedicated snow-removal machine may be the better investment.

    Industry observers note that it depends on how you use the word. While “riding mower” and “lawn tractor” are often interchangeable, there are key differences between the two pieces of equipment. A riding mower typically means any mower you sit on, including a lawn tractor or zero-turn mower. Nevertheless, a lawn/garden tractor will generally be more expensive and have a larger, sturdier frame. Lawn/garden tractors are designed and built to accept manufacturers’ compatible direct-fit attachments and accessories.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Recent findings suggest that plaintiff Matt Gioia moved his family from Colorado to Maine in the summer of 2020 to start a new church.
    • Gioia sought space from the Hermon School Department, which generally opens up its facilities to various groups:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this happened when the board was deciding whether to allow a long-term lease of space on weekends to a church, pursuant to a policy that allowed such leases for community groups generally. And, a federal court held Friday, this violated the First Amendment. Some excerpts from the long opinion in Pines Church v. Hermon School Dep't, by Chief Judge Lance Walker (D. Me.):.

    Recent findings suggest that plaintiff Matt Gioia moved his family from Colorado to Maine in the summer of 2020 to start a new church. Gioia was born in Waterville, Maine, and lived in Guilford, Maine until he graduated high school and joined the military at seventeen years old. Initially, Gioia's church—The Pines Church—gathered at his home. In March of 2021, The Pines Church began holding Sunday morning services at a movie theater in Orono, Maine, pursuant to a month-to-month lease arrangement. As the Church grew, Gioia began to look for a new space that could accommodate a larger group.

    Gioia sought space from the Hermon School Department, which generally opens up its facilities to various groups:.

    This policy provides that "[s]chool facilities should be made available for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities." The policy distinguishes between "occasional or short-term use of school facilities," which "shall be authorized by the school principal," and "long-term rental or lease," which "shall be authorized by the Hermon School Committee upon the recommendation of the Superintendent of Schools.".

    But the Hermon School Committee (which consisted of "Committee Chair Jesse Keith, Vice Chair Karen Shorey, Stephanie Oiler, Haily Keezer, and Christopher McLaughlin") denied the Church's request for a year-long or six-month lease, allowing only a month-to-month lease (which appeared to be inadequate for the church, given its need for a stable meeting location). Here's part of the summary of the facts, based on the bench trial that the court held:.

    The next day [after a hearing], a former committee member emailed Keith and Shorey to share her belief "that it is not in our communities [sic] best interest to lease one of our school facilities to any religious organization," warning that "[t]here is a quiet movement in our country by some conservative religious groups who are actively working to soften the boundaries between church/state, starting with our schools" and that granting the Church a lease would lead to "a slippery slope." She wondered how the Hermon School Department would have to respond to a similar request from "an Imam who wants to open a mosque," in light of the "precedent" set by a lease to The Pines Church.

    Her email concluded with unintended irony: "There's a reason why the founding fathers wrote the constitution the way they did." Keith and Shorey denied at trial that this email influenced their decision-making with respect to the Church's lease request, which I find implausible in light of the trial record….

    McLaughlin reached out to [HSD Superintendent Micah] Grant and explained that he "had a few additional questions" for Gioia:.

    McLaughlin "wanted to get a better sense of how [T]he Pines Church approaches problems of diversity, equity, and inclusion around their messaging around some key issues relevant to marginalized communities." Those questions requested information about the Church's views on same-sex marriage, "[a]ccess to safe and affordable abortion," "[a]ccess to gender affirming medical care," "[c]onversion therapy for LGBTQIA+ individuals (youth and adults)," and "[i]nclusive sexual education and access to birth control for youth." ….

    Recent findings suggest that [At a later meeting, High School Principal Brian] Walsh took the podium and explained that he had several reservations about the Church's request. He first explained that it would be difficult to find the staff to clean the building on Sunday afternoons. But apart from this, he continued:.

    Recent findings suggest that [W]e've never had a long-term lease, at least over my twenty-one years here, and I think there's a number of reasons we don't do that. There's a lot of variables we just don't know. No question our students should come first, our program should come first.

    We also don't know or have the sense of how this will be promoted, to [the student representative's] question. If you put Hermon High School's name with a church or another organization with different beliefs than the school has, I see that as problematic. But again, that's where I sit and that's where I stand. Doesn't mean this organization won't do a great job, doesn't mean they won't support, hopefully, our mission as well. I just don't know, there are too many variables with that and again we have not—we have never done that.

    It has been revealed that what I would not want is for students to feel like a group organization that we are renting to, their vision or their mission is now ours. And there's a blurred line when it comes to that. I have nothing against this church, this reverend, or anything, we've just never said yes to something like this, so probably why it's in your hands, because you guys get to make that decision. I'm looking at the facility and some other variables, so that's kind of—that's where I come from….

    Industry observers note that [At a later meeting,] Oiler then made a motion for a month-to-month lease, citing concerns about the number of people and cleaning the space afterwards, which she was careful to emphasize had nothing to do with the organization. Keezer asked if they could ask Gioia about how the Church kept its current space clean. Oiler curiously protested that this was not about the Church (when in fact it was ostensibly about the Church and its janitorial readiness) but any organization, then adding the less than persuasive point that if fifteen people got the stomach bug at the same time, someone would have to clean it up. {At trial, Oiler testified that she had in mind a specific incident that occurred at Hermon Middle School when one of her children was a student there.}.

    Given the shortage of custodial staffing, she explained, she was concerned about the number of people who would be coming in and out of the building. She suggested that the Committee investigate its current rental arrangements, to make sure those organizations were paying what they should considering the costs associated with hosting them. What this had to do with the Church's application remains a mystery….

    It has been revealed that the Free Speech Clause prohibits restrictions on access to limited or designated public fora that "discriminate against speech on the basis of viewpoint," including on the basis that the viewpoint in question is a religious one. In other words, if a public school's facilities are available for public use, a religious organization cannot be denied access to those facilities because it is a religious organization. Similarly, the Free Exercise Clause "bars even 'subtle departures from neutrality' on matters of religion," and therefore prohibits "denying a generally available benefit solely on account of religious identity," unless such denial is "justified … by a state interest 'of the highest order.'" ….

    By virtue of Policy KG, the Hermon School Department made its facilities available "for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities," including for "long-term rental or lease." Having done so, the School Department could not then reject the Church's lease application because it is a religious organization or because of disagreement with its religious viewpoints, without violating the First Amendment, as Plaintiffs contend has occurred….

    The court concluded that the Department indeed violate the Church's First Amendment rights, by discriminating against it based on its "religious viewpoint or out of animus against that viewpoint":.

    I start with the question of whether a majority or significant block of committee members demonstrated bad motive.

    According to recent reports, I find without any difficulty that McLaughlin exhibited bad motive. McLaughlin's intrusive questions expressed viewpoint related concerns towards Plaintiffs, and he was the only member not to vote in favor of any lease term, including the month-to-month arrangement. Although his email itemizing political and cultural questions occurred early in the process, before the Committee received any advice from counsel, and even though he testified that he harbored no ill will toward Plaintiffs after gaining more information about them, it strikes me as very likely that McLaughlin lacked objectivity when it came to the question of leasing school space to the Church.

    It appears that he based his decision directly on the Plaintiffs' religious beliefs and its associated political and culture ethics that flow from those beliefs, and the religious nature of the proposed use. McLaughlin would have approached a lease request differently had it been presented by an organization that shared his personal beliefs.

    Sources indicate that I also find that Oiler was unable to overcome concerns over constitutionally permissible school-church association, notwithstanding the legal advice the Committee received, and Grant repeatedly emphasized. Though less openly hostile than McLaughlin, Oiler's attitude toward the Church was anything but neutral…. [I]t struck me during her testimony, and I find, that Oiler's chief concern was that the tenant would be a Church. This was made only more obvious by protesting far too much that this was not about the Church but instead fear, for example, of mass vomiting epidemics and the platoon of janitorial assistance that would be required to mop it up.

    All of her other concerns about space and the like were definitively answered by Grant as not remotely problematic. I find based on the trial record that her motive was to avoid the School's association with the Church for its religious views. The First Amendment is designed to avoid discriminatory treatment of religious organizations in their enjoyment of the benefits of public facilities based on their religious beliefs or speech. For this reason, I find that Oiler, like McLaughlin, voted as she did based on "bad motive.".

    I find that Plaintiffs have proved that bad motive prevented Shorey from approaching the lease question fairly. Shorey, at her deposition, suggested that she believed McLaughlin's culture war email was appropriate, even though she later sought to characterize it as inappropriate at trial.

    It may be that Shorey believes that a School Committee should have the discretion to question any organization about how its values align with what she sees as the school community's values, to the extent a school community has its own conflicting body of values that can be reduced to a catechesis—perhaps it does. But support for a process that involves examining a prospective tenant's views on religious problems, simply because the prospective tenant is a church, tends rather starkly to highlight the questioner's lack of neutrality toward religion….

    Although I find that a majority of voting members exhibited bad motive which would itself be sufficient to end the inquiry, my findings should be considered also in context of the discussion during the deliberative process, which included rather openly anti-religious organization sentiment expressed by Walsh at least as he served as a voice of the school community and the discomfort it might experience especially if the beliefs of the School, whatever those might be, and the Church were at loggerheads. Even if the record had not established a majority of voting members acting out of bad motive, it would still have constituted a significant bloc of legislators and "circumstances suggesting the probable complicity of others," as well as "evidence indicating that the legislators bowed to an impermissible community animus.".

    Recall that Walsh passed along student concerns about the Church qua church using the School and when asked if any spoke supportively of the idea, Walsh reported that none had. Also recall the email received by Keith Shorey from a former committee member. That former member insisted that this was all a Trojan horse coordinated by conservative Christian groups to blur the line between school and religion. What would the Committee do, the former committee member queried, if an Imam were to set up shop at Hermon High School next?

    The standard is one of likelihood, and on that basis, I find that at least three of the five decision makers acted under the influence of bad motive and in so doing violated the Plaintiffs' rights under the First Amendment….

    Defendant points to the majority vote in favor of a month-to-month use arrangement as proof of the lack of bias on the part of its committee members. I agree with the Church that this was not persuasive evidence of a lack of bad motive but to the contrary, is evidence of bad motive. The Committee knew the Church required a more fixed arrangement before uprooting itself from its then current location than a month-to-month arrangement provides. This appears to me to have been an offer designed to be rejected not one born of wholesome support for the Free Exercise Clause….

    In a recent development, bethany Onishenko and Robert H. Tyler (Tyler Law LLP), Erin Mersino and Julianne E. Fleischer (Advocates for Faith and Freedom), Joel L. Oster (Oster Law Firm), Wenonah Wirick (Conley & Wirick, P.A.) represent plaintiffs.

    Industry observers note that modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

    Though in wintertime a window seat affords postcard-perfect views of snow-covered tree branches, it’s not necessarily the most comfortable perch on a cold day. During the chilly season, so much heat can escape through the panes of glass as well as through any cracks or gaps around the window frame that you’ll want to wrap up in a blanket, or at least put on a sweater, before you risk sitting so close to a window. The Energy Information Administration reports that the average home loses as much as a third of its energy as a result of poor window insulation. Luckily, there are several ways to mitigate this loss. Follow these best practices for how to insulate windows, and you can secure a warmer winter with just one weekend of work.

    Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

    According to recent reports, decades of exposure to the elements can wear away one of your main defenses against heat loss: exterior caulking. Once this begins to crumble, cracks can start to form around the window frame. If your windows are drafty, take swift action to replace the exterior caulking along the window frames before the weather takes a turn for the worse.

    Sources indicate that check the weather before you begin the process. For successful application of caulking, you’ll want clear skies for 24 hours—no snow or rain—and, ideally, temperatures above 45 degrees Fahrenheit.

    Use a putty knife to scrape window edges clean out the old caulking and peeling paint. Then, wipe the surface clean of any remnants with a damp rag. Let the surface dry for a few hours so the newly introduced caulking will readily adhere. It’s best to start the project early in the day to allow enough dry time. You could also leave it to dry overnight.

    Recent findings suggest that load your no-drip caulking gun with a cartridge of silicone exterior caulk and hold it at a 45-degree angle in order to get deep into the cracks around the window frame. Apply a solid, continuous bead of caulking between the frame and the siding, all the way around the window. Any caulk that oozes out of the crack should be pushed in gently with a putty knife.

    Allow this to cure overnight to provide the best protection from wind and moisture.

    The sash, the part of the window that moves to open and close, is the area most homeowners zero in on when they’re trying to improve window insulation. While this area is key, don’t neglect the glass itself or ignore other draft-curbing solutions. Take a multistep approach to insulating the inside of your windows by employing weatherstripping, window film, and energy-smart window treatments. Though we present this step-by-step approach as a process, you’ll still gain energy savings if you don’t complete every step.

    Note: When you’re selecting replacement weatherstripping, closely consider the pros and cons of each material. As with many building materials, you get what you pay for in terms of lifespan. Felt, for example, is a common pick for its low price, but it can fail within only a few years. Adhesive-backed foam and tubular gasket stripping, on the other hand, are both cost-effective compression seals that work reliably and provide 3 to 5 years of protection from the cold.

    If your weatherstripping is worn or crumbling, it’s time to remove and replace it. Adhesive-backed stripping can simply be pulled up by hand. If the weatherstripping is attached with nails or screws, however, you must first remove the fasteners with a claw hammer or drill before you can lift it away. Once you’ve pulled the weatherstripping off, wipe down the window sash with a damp rag or paper towels and household cleaner. Allow it to dry thoroughly.

    Measure your sash carefully, then cut the weatherstripping of your choice to length. Start as close as you can to the end of one side of the sash, peel off any adhesive backing, then carefully press the weatherstripping into place on the sash, making your way carefully to the other end.

    “One insulating technique I love and have done many times requires the trim to be off (if, say, you’re installing a latest window or entry door): fill the voids between the door or window jamb and the rough framing with low-expanding foam insulation.”.

    —Mark Clement, Contributing Writer.

    With the upcoming weatherstripping in place, you’ll want to double up your efforts with a window insulation kit. In addition to retaining up to 55 percent of your home’s heat in winter, this type of window covering will reflect heat and block UV rays from passing through uncovered windows, lowering indoor temperatures in summer and saving energy costs year-round. Before you proceed, check to see if your windows are still under warranty; the addition of window film may void the contract. If you’re in the clear, select the best quality insulating window film you can find for the job. Cheap versions can make the outdoors seem darker and even somewhat blurry. While that’s not a major problem for windows in some rooms, for more prominent windows, you may want to invest in higher-quality film that causes little to no loss of clarity and light.

    According to recent reports, note: Cheaper methods that produce a similar insulating effect involve heat-and-shrink film or even bubble wrap, but these are often less attractive options that hamper or prevent the use of the windows, or hinder visibility. These inexpensive fixes, however, can be effective, easy to apply, and energy-efficient solutions for basement or attic windows.

    Industry observers note that whichever method you choose, installation instructions vary from product to product. In general, start by washing the windowpanes so that no dust or lint gets trapped during application, then follow the manufacturer’s directions for installing the window film.

    Best Home blackout curtains keep out up to 99% of light with triple-weave polyester construction and a layer of black yarn. Read the review.

    In a recent development, for one last defense against heat loss and drafts, consider hanging thermal curtains. For best insulating effects, install the curtain rod above and past each window on either side so the curtains fully cover the window frame. If it’s not appropriately installed, make adjustments to the rod’s position to maximize heat retention. While other window treatments like blinds or sheers offer some protection from drafts, a set of heavy curtains that you draw shut after dusk can cut heat loss by up to 17 percent.

    Sources indicate that whether you ultimately decide to complete just one or all of these steps, you’ll still reap benefits. The more solutions you employ, however, the greater heat retention and energy savings you’ll see, and potentially not just in winter, but all year-round. If you’ve tried all these methods and still have poor window insulation, it might be time to replace your home’s windows.

    That’s where a sewer inspection camera can help. Instead of just guessing, plumbers, drain-cleaning technicians and experienced property owners can visually inspect accessible portions of a line for signs of root intrusion, buildup, standing water, cracks, offsets and other visible problems before deciding what comes next.

    In a recent development, the SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera is designed for those longer, more demanding inspections. A rigid push cable, self-leveling camera and bright adjustable lighting help operators work farther into sewer lines while recording what they find along the way.

    The SANYIPACE S830ASMKT sewer camera is a professional-grade pipe inspection system built to provide a clear view inside longer drain and sewer lines.

The added stiffness gives you the pushing support needed to move the camera through longer pipe runs, although actual reach will depend on the diameter, bends, layout and condition of the line.

    At the end of the cable is a 31-millimeter self-leveling camera head. The self-leveling design keeps the image upright as the camera rotates inside the pipe, making footage easier to interpret than video that constantly spins as the cable moves.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Readers may recall the story of Karyann Parkinson, the Williamsburg mother (and law student) who was criminally prosecuted for letting her young child walk to a neighborhood pond to collect goose feathers. As I recounted in The Free Press, Parkinson was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, a first-degree misdemeanor in Virginia, because the authorities thought her child was too young to take a walk. The judge sentenced her to six-months in jail, but suspended the sentence. An appeal is pending.

    It has been revealed that as a consequence of her conviction, Parkinson was added to Virginia's Child Abuse and Neglect Registry, where she will be listed for the next seven years. Parkinson also feared that the conviction could prevent her from practicing law.

    In a recent development, prosecutors brought the charges against Parkinson while she was preparing to take the Virginia Bar exam, and her conviction came while her character and fitness application was under review. It is common to place character and fitness evaluations on hold pending the outcome of legal or disciplinary proceedings, and Parkinson initially received a communication to that effect.

    Industry observers note that upon review of the details of Parkinson's case, however, the Virginia Board of Bar Examiners concluded that nothing alleged against Parkinson cast doubt on her character and fitness to practice law in the Commonwealth of Virginia, and her application was approved. The Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney should take note.

    While the Virginia Bar authorities recognized that Parkinson's actions were not the sort of thing that should prevent bar admission, the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney apparently believes that Parkinson's actions were worth criminal prosecution--with all that entails. In this case, that meant police officers had to spend half a day of paid time (if not time and a half) sitting in a courthouse when they could have been out on the street responding to community needs. They will do it again in February when a court will hear Parkinson's appeal (which will take the form of a de novo jury trial, given how Virginia handles such cases). Williamsburg and James City County are reasonably safe communities, but is this really the best way to allocate law enforcement resources?

    No doubt some prosecutions for child endangerment are motivated for a concern about a child's safety, but it is hard to credit such a justification here. The Commonwealth Attorney's office waited two weeks to file charges after the initial incident, but not because it was gathering evidence or conducting any sort of investigation. Rather, as one of the police officers testified at trial, it was because Parkinson was pregnant, so they thought it was reasonable to wait. (Yet she was still charged before giving birth, natch.) As I noted in my Free Press piece, it is hard not to conclude Parkinson's real offense was being insufficiently obsequious to the authorities.

    Recent findings suggest that upon review, the Virginia Board of Bar Examiners realized that Parkinson's actions did not justify delaying (let alone preventing) her admission to the Virginia Bar. With more time to consider the case (and the outrage it has engendered) perhaps the Williamsburg Commonwealth Attorney should reconsider the continued prosecution of Parkinson for what was, at worst, a debatable parenting choice. Confessing error and asking the court to vacate the conviction would seem to be a better use of tax dollars and public resources than continuing to pursue this case.

    Before or After the Snow? Here’s the Right Time to Salt Your Driveway This Winter

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.
    • The Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months.
    • According to recent reports, it depends.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.

    The Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months. Icy sidewalks, stairs and driveways are largely to blame for this seasonal uptick. Icy driveways are not only dangerous to walk on but also make driving and parking difficult. Ice melt salt is one of the best ways to keep driveways clear, but how should you best use it? Should you apply it before or after a storm — or both? Two industry experts weigh in on the best way to salt your driveway for optimal results this winter.

    According to recent reports, it depends. Salting before a big storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.

    It has been revealed that plan to apply salt several hours before a storm hits for best results. It creates a salty coating that prevents the initial snowfall from bonding with the driveway surface. Pre-salting reduces total snow accumulation and makes snow removal easier once the storm is over. Avoid doing it too far in advance, or if rain is in the forecast, as the salt can be washed or blown away before the snow arrives. It’s not necessary to salt before a light snowfall of less than six inches.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s always a good idea to salt after it snows, but don’t rely on it to replace snow removal efforts. First remove as much snow as possible with a shovel or snowblower, then use salt to clear away any remaining slush and snow.

    In a recent development, the best time to salt is immediately after snow removal, before cold nighttime temperatures set in. “When applied before the temperatures drop, salt prevents ice from forming and ensures the snow does not freeze solid to the ground,” Angelika Klimorowski, a winter maintenance specialist at Online Rock Salt, notes.

    Apply salt before and after a big storm for best results, especially when heavy snow, sleet or freezing rain is expected.

    “Pre-salting helps prevent ice from bonding to the driveway, while a second application can help break down any ice that forms,” Aaron Strickland, owner of Mr. Trim Lawn & Garden Services, states. “For a typical snowfall, both applications usually aren’t necessary.”.

    If only a few inches of snow is forecast, salting after snow removal is likely sufficient. Applying salt before and after a small storm is not only a waste of money, but can damage driveway surfaces, burn lawn edges and generate harmful storm runoff.

    Sources indicate that “The exact amount of rock salt that you need will depend on how big the area is that you are planning to de-ice,” Klimorowski claims. A little goes a long way, and more is not better. A 12-oz. coffee mug filled with salt is enough to treat a 1,000-sq.-ft. driveway. Spread salt evenly, leaving about 3 inches between salt grains. Avoid overapplication, as it can degrade driveway surfaces and harm the environment.

    A handheld spreader makes application easier and more consistent, especially for larger driveways. “We try to follow recommended coverage rates and use a spreader wherever possible,” Strickland states. “Too much salt wastes product and can damage surrounding grass and gardens.” If spreading salt by hand, always wear gloves and cascade it for even coverage.

    Rock salt is only effective down to ground temperatures of 15 to 17 degrees. Don’t apply more salt if it’s not working, as it’s likely too cold out for it to work. “If your area tends to experience colder temperatures, you may need to find an alternative de-icing product to keep your surfaces safe,” Klimorowski states. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melt products are two common alternatives that remain effective at sub-zero temperatures.

    Recent findings suggest that yes, rain will wash away salt rather than dissolve it. It then ends up in storm drains and potentially pollutes local bodies of water.

    Rock salt stops working in temperatures below 10 to 15 degrees.

    “While it is true that salt will work best if you apply it before the temperatures drop, there is no deadline, and you can always apply it later,” Klimorowski says.

    According to recent reports, there’s no guarantee salt will damage your driveway, but you should use it sparingly. Concrete driveways are particularly vulnerable to salt damage.

    #44407. How to Shovel the Trickiest Surfaces the Right Way, From Pavers to Your Roof
